Design Palette

Design Book

1,220 sq ft · 2 bed / 3 bath

A black-and-white checkerboard floor, set on the diagonal, runs through the entire home — bedrooms, both upstairs bathrooms, living room, kitchen, dining room, entryways, closets — at one consistent size throughout, stopping only at the downstairs bath, where a small-format alabaster mosaic takes the whole floor, paired with jade green tiled walls and matte black hardware. The primary bedroom gets a pair of twin beds, plus a power recline love seat. The secondary bedroom gets full bed. The downstairs powder room is converted into a full bath with a neo-angle corner shower, and the living room gets a matching power recline sofa and storage coffee table.

A note on flexibility. The one must-have is the checkerboard tile throughout. Everything else — colors, materials, fixtures, and how to get the best value — is genuinely open to the design firm's judgment. This palette is a starting reference, not a locked spec. The general aesthetic direction we're after: fresh and current, the kind of space that photographs well today, but grounded enough in timeless choices that it won't read as dated in five or ten years.
By Room Material callouts and specifications
Primary Bedroom

Two separate twin beds give the kids who sleep here their own space. A power recline sleeper love seat sits between them for guests. The 13-foot wall behind both headboards and the sofa is wrapped floor to ceiling in the same wood-look plank tile used on the entryway wall, run vertically in 13 columns to pull the eye up — a durable, wipeable surface right where beds and furniture make contact. Checkerboard floor, gray walls in glossy finish elsewhere in the room. Closets stay open — doors come off, frames stay in place — fitted with built-in organizers and a built-in desktop. All hardware in matte black.

Reference image — wood slat accent wall behind a bed, paired with black hardware (sconces, nightstands, lamp). Same wood-slat language used elsewhere in the house; not a locked spec, just a mood reference.

Primary Bathroom

Alcove tub / tile shower with matte black drain kit, right drain, and a curved shower curtain rod. Soft jade ceramic in a glossy glaze — Mila, Jade, set in a straight 4" grid — wraps the tub surround and carries straight on down the whole wall that holds the vanity and toilet, floor to ceiling — one continuous plane rather than a patch behind the mirror. Single 36" vanity, Acorn finish, black hardware provides unobstructed width to the tub's full alcove opening. Checkerboard floor, gray walls, matte black faucet, medicine cabinet, toilet, shower head + handheld wand for tub use.

Downstairs Bathroom

Powder room converted to a full bath. The floor changes at the threshold: checkerboard stops at the door, and a soft alabaster small-format mosaic takes over the room, running up to a low curb at the shower. A custom neo-angle shower — 37" x 31", the smallest that clears code — tucks into the southwest corner behind a 22" frameless glass door, hinged to swing outward. Jade green glossy ceramic, the same Mila, Jade used in both suite baths, runs floor-to-ceiling up the whole west and south walls — both carry a wet fixture along their length, not just the shower — in a straight 4" grid. Inside: a custom mud-set pan sloped to a matte black point drain, a tall recessed niche trimmed in matte black on the short (west) leg, and a matte black rain head + handheld wand centered on the long (south) leg — more elbow room for washing and shampooing than the short leg gave. North of the shower, the toilet sits against the west wall. The sink gets its own spot on the south wall: a West Elm Ellington vanity, cylindrical fluted cabinet with a round vessel top, and a tall gooseneck faucet to clear its raised rim. Medicine cabinet above, same toilet used elsewhere in the house. The entry converts to a pocket door, satin black to match the house standard — no swing to fight in a tight room.

Proposed layout, drawn to scale in the same style as the reference: actual 61" x 61" room. Toilet in the north nook, centerline 15" off the north wall. Neo-angle shower, 37" x 31", ≈1,026 sq in interior, with a 22" glass door swinging outward. Vanity/basin on the south wall in the resulting 24" strip east of the shower. Walls drawn at real 2x4 + drywall thickness, which gives the recessed niche its actual depth. Entry is a 28" pocket door on the east wall, shown half-open — the opening shifts 5" off the north wall so a full 28" of cavity remains to the south. Best-effort schematic, not a stamped construction drawing — verify on site before anything is cut.

Reference image — the darker Jaden, Hunter option installed (the original pick; see appendix), run vertical, two walls meeting at a corner. Fittings shown are brass and there is a recessed niche; ours are matte black, our corner is a 31″ x 37″ neo-angle rather than a straight run, and ours now runs floor-to-ceiling across the full west and south walls, not just the shower.

Entryway

An archway passageway wall between the living room and kitchen. A tiled accent wall — wood-look ribbed ceramic in a plank format — wraps up and over the small ceiling section above it, reading as one clean, continuous statement; the long run of wall is exactly what the plank proportion and relief texture need to shine. Optional: a shoe storage bench along the wall. Checkerboard floors, gray walls elsewhere in the room.

Under-Stairs Walk-In Closet

An empty under-stairs closet, fitted out with a mix of hanging rods and open shelving, a wall-mounted vacuum charging dock, and a dedicated light fixture (previously unlit). General-purpose storage. Checkerboard floor, gray walls in glossy finish, matte black hardware.

Reference image — full-depth layout with hanging rods on both sloped sides, a center column of drawers with a pull-out shoe rack, and open shelving up top. Looks AI-generated/stylized rather than a real product photo, but the zone mix (double-hang + drawers + shoe storage) is the useful part.

Reference image — the actual constraint in a space like this: the stepped stair-stringer ceiling in a narrow under-stairs run, tapering down to nothing at the far end. Useful for judging how much of the depth is usable at standing height vs. crouching height.

Reference image — sloped ceiling treated as a feature (herringbone wood cladding) instead of hidden, with open shelving on the tall end and cabinetry where the ceiling drops. The arch and stone counter are more than we need here, but the shelving-to-cabinet transition following the slope is the relevant idea.

Appendix Bathroom wall tile options
Bathroom Wall Tile Options

Five wall tile options compared for the three bathrooms — on reflectance, price, format, and how each pairs with the Leona checkerboard floor (white squares ≈85% reflectance, black squares ≈16%, both warm in undertone despite reading as neutral). Mila, Jade is the tile now specified throughout this book — chosen over the original pick, Jaden, Hunter. The price and format deltas below are still quoted against Hunter, the original baseline.

Deep emerald, true green, glossy. Darkest of the five options.

Against the checkerboard: At 18% it sits almost exactly on Nero Marquina's own value — only 2 points apart (+2 / −67 to the white squares) — and its 134° blue-emerald hue runs cooler than the floor's warm undertone.

Lightest of the five options and glossy. Warmer hue than Hunter (92° vs 134°), closer to the floor's own warm undertone.

Against the checkerboard: At 54% it lands almost exactly halfway between the checkerboard's black and white squares (+38 / −31) — a genuine third value, not a near-match to either extreme — and it stays glossy, keeping the glossy-wall/matte-floor sheen contrast.

Cheapest by a wide margin, nearly Mila's exact hue. Matte finish and a much bigger plank than Hunter's — the boldest single element in the room if used.

Against the checkerboard: At 41% it clears the black squares comfortably (+25 / −44), but matte against a matte floor flattens the sheen contrast, and a 6"x24" plank is bolder than the floor's own 12" checkers.

Closest match to Hunter's own proportions (same width, just shorter pieces), so the vertical-column look translates most directly. Priciest of the five.

Against the checkerboard: At 43% it clears both extremes (+27 / −42) with the warmest hue of the five (100°). Matte, so it loses Hunter's glossy sheen against the floor — but its 2.5" width means the room's column composition carries over most directly.

Added after spotting it installed: strong piece-to-piece shade variation — pale sage squares scattered among blue-teals — under a wavy high-gloss glaze. The coolest hue on this page (163°, past even Hunter's 134°), leaning teal rather than jade. Cheapest after Dax.

Against the checkerboard: At 49% it sits comfortably between the black and white squares (+33 / −36), nearly as balanced as Mila — but its cool teal hue pulls against the floor's warm undertone, where Mila leans with it.

Summary. Hunter is the darkest option on this page and runs cooler than the checkerboard floor's warm marbling. Mila is the lightest of the four, keeps a glossy finish, and its warm hue sits closest to the floor's own undertone, though it's a small square rather than a plank. Dax is the least expensive by far but matte and a much larger plank. Ellie keeps Hunter's plank width most closely but is matte and the most expensive per square foot. Lilah, added after it was spotted installed, is nearly as balanced as Mila in value and second-cheapest, but reads teal — the coolest hue of the five, pulling against the floor's warm undertone. Each carries a different trade-off among reflectance, price, format, and finish.
